column9: When a biologist says a process is aerobic, what does that mean?
column14: It makes oxygen
column15: It needs oxygen
column16: It happens only in plants
column17: It happens without any glucose
column28: Aerobic means "with air," so an aerobic process needs oxygen. Aerobic respiration uses oxygen up; it does not make it. A common mistake is mixing this up with photosynthesis, which is the process that gives off oxygen.
column29: Think of an aerobics class. What gas are you breathing in hard?

column9: Cellular respiration that can happen without oxygen is called ___ respiration.
column28: Anaerobic means "without air (oxygen)." The prefix an- means without. A common mistake is writing aerobic, which is the type that needs oxygen.
column29: Add a two-letter prefix that means "without" to the front of aerobic.

column9: Anaerobic respiration has two stages. What are they?
column14: The Krebs cycle and the electron transport chain
column15: Glycolysis and the Krebs cycle
column16: Glycolysis and fermentation
column17: Fermentation and the electron transport chain
column28: Anaerobic respiration is glycolysis followed by fermentation, and both happen in the cytoplasm. The Krebs cycle and electron transport chain need oxygen, so they belong to aerobic respiration only. A common mistake is picking any pair that has fermentation in it.
column29: Which stages can still run when there is no oxygen at all?

column9: Which stage is the same first step in both aerobic and anaerobic respiration?
column14: Electron transport chain
column15: Glycolysis
column16: Krebs cycle
column17: Fermentation
column28: Glycolysis splits glucose in the cytoplasm and does not need oxygen, so cells start both kinds of respiration with it. What happens next depends on whether oxygen is there. A common mistake is choosing fermentation, but fermentation comes after glycolysis and only when oxygen is missing.
column29: It's the stage that happens before the cell "finds out" whether oxygen is around.

column9: In aerobic respiration, the Krebs cycle and the electron transport chain take place in which organelle?
column14: Nucleus
column15: Chloroplast
column16: Ribosome
column17: Mitochondrion
column28: The Krebs cycle runs in the mitochondrial matrix, and the electron transport chain runs on the inner membrane of the mitochondrion. That's why aerobic respiration needs mitochondria and fermentation doesn't. A common mistake is choosing the chloroplast, which is where photosynthesis happens.
column29: Which organelle is nicknamed the powerhouse of the cell?

column9: A muscle cell is short on oxygen and switches to fermentation. Where in the cell does fermentation happen?
column14: The mitochondrial matrix
column15: The cytoplasm (cytosol)
column16: The nucleus
column17: The ribosomes
column28: Fermentation, like glycolysis, happens in the cytoplasm (also called the cytosol). It never goes into the mitochondria. A common mistake is picking the mitochondria because they are linked to energy, but only aerobic respiration uses them.
column29: Fermentation doesn't use the powerhouse organelle. Where else in the cell could it be?

column9: Lactobacillus bacteria in milk break down one glucose molecule by fermentation. What is the net ATP gained?
column14: 0 ATP
column15: 2 ATP
column16: 6 ATP
column17: About 36 ATP
column28: Fermentation nets only 2 ATP per glucose, and they all come from glycolysis. About 36 is what aerobic respiration makes. A common mistake is choosing 0, thinking that "no oxygen" means "no energy."
column29: Fermentation only gets the ATP that glycolysis makes.

column9: Anaerobic respiration releases no usable energy for the cell.
column28: False. Anaerobic respiration does release energy: it nets 2 ATP per glucose. That's far less than aerobic respiration (about 36), but it is enough to keep cells going for a short time. A common mistake is thinking "no oxygen" means "no energy."
column29: Think about how your muscles keep working for a few seconds even when they are out of oxygen.

column9: How does anaerobic respiration compare with aerobic respiration?
column14: It is slower and makes more ATP per glucose
column15: It is faster and makes more ATP per glucose
column16: It is faster but makes much less ATP per glucose
column17: It is the same speed and makes the same ATP per glucose
column28: Anaerobic respiration makes ATP quickly because it skips the Krebs cycle and electron transport chain, but it nets only 2 ATP per glucose instead of about 36. Aerobic is slower but far more efficient. A common mistake is thinking "faster" also means "more."
column29: Think of a sprint: quick energy, but you can't keep it up for long.

column9: Which product is made by alcoholic fermentation but NOT by lactic acid fermentation?
column14: ATP
column15: Glucose
column16: Carbon dioxide
column17: Pyruvate
column28: Alcoholic fermentation makes ethanol and carbon dioxide (plus 2 ATP). Lactic acid fermentation makes only lactic acid and 2 ATP, with no gas. Both make ATP, and both make pyruvate first during glycolysis. A common mistake is choosing ATP, but every type of respiration makes some ATP.
column29: Which kind of fermentation makes bread dough puff up with bubbles?

column9: Which product is made by aerobic respiration but by neither type of fermentation?
column14: Water
column15: ATP
column16: Carbon dioxide
column17: Ethanol
column28: Water forms at the end of the electron transport chain, when oxygen picks up electrons and hydrogen, so only aerobic respiration makes it. Carbon dioxide is also made by alcoholic fermentation, and ATP is made by all of them. A common mistake is choosing carbon dioxide and forgetting that yeast fermentation releases it too.
column29: Cross off anything that yeast or muscle cells also make when they ferment.

column9: Which organism is best known for alcoholic fermentation?
column14: A sunflower
column15: Lactobacillus bacteria
column16: Baker's yeast
column17: A human muscle cell
column28: Yeast (a fungus) ferments sugar into ethanol and carbon dioxide, which is used to make bread and ethanol fuel. Lactobacillus and human muscle cells use lactic acid fermentation instead. A common mistake is picking human muscle cells; humans do not make alcohol when they ferment.
column29: Which one do bakers buy in little packets?

column9: Which food is made with the help of lactic acid fermentation by bacteria?
column14: Yogurt
column15: Orange juice
column16: Hard-boiled eggs
column17: Popcorn
column28: Bacteria such as Lactobacillus ferment the sugar in milk into lactic acid, which makes yogurt thick and tangy. The other foods are not made by fermentation. A common mistake is thinking only alcoholic fermentation is used to make food.
column29: Which food is made by adding live bacteria cultures to milk?

column9: Cabbage can become sauerkraut or coleslaw. Which one is made by letting bacteria ferment the cabbage in a sealed jar of salty brine, and why does it taste sour?
column14: Coleslaw, because the cabbage stays raw and crunchy
column15: Sauerkraut, because bacteria make lactic acid
column16: Coleslaw, because bacteria make carbon dioxide
column17: Sauerkraut, because yeast make ethanol
column28: Sauerkraut is cabbage fermented by lactic acid bacteria in brine; the lactic acid makes it sour and keeps it from spoiling. Coleslaw is just raw cabbage in dressing. A common mistake is thinking the sour taste comes from yeast and alcohol.
column29: Sauer is the German word for sour. What kind of acid makes food sour?

column9: Factories in the Midwest turn corn sugar into ethanol fuel that is mixed into gasoline. Which process makes the ethanol?
column14: Lactic acid fermentation by bacteria
column15: Aerobic respiration in mitochondria
column16: Photosynthesis in corn leaves
column17: Alcoholic fermentation by yeast
column28: Yeast ferment the sugar from corn into ethanol and carbon dioxide; ethanol is the alcohol in E10 gasoline. Lactic acid fermentation never makes ethanol, and aerobic respiration breaks sugar all the way down to carbon dioxide and water. A common mistake is choosing photosynthesis because the corn made the sugar, but the ethanol comes later, from yeast.
column29: Which organism makes ethanol when it breaks down sugar without oxygen?

column9: A baker forgets to add yeast to a batch of bread dough. Why does that dough stay flat?
column14: Without yeast, no carbon dioxide gas is made to puff up the dough
column15: Without yeast, no oxygen gas is made to puff up the dough as it bakes
column16: Without yeast, no lactic acid is made to puff up the dough in the oven
column17: Without yeast, the flour cannot soak up any water
column28: Yeast ferment sugar into ethanol and carbon dioxide. The carbon dioxide gas gets trapped in the dough as bubbles, so the dough rises; the ethanol bakes off in the oven. A common mistake is saying oxygen, but fermentation does not make oxygen.
column29: Which gas does alcoholic fermentation release?

column9: Which activity depends most on anaerobic respiration in your leg muscles?
column14: Walking slowly around the block for 30 minutes with a friend
column15: Running up three flights of stairs as fast as you can
column16: Standing in the lunch line
column17: Riding a bike at an easy pace for an hour on a flat trail
column28: An all-out burst uses ATP faster than your blood can deliver oxygen, so muscle cells add lactic acid fermentation to make ATP quickly. Slow, steady activities run on aerobic respiration because oxygen keeps up. A common mistake is thinking long activities are anaerobic just because they are tiring.
column29: Which one would leave you gasping for air in under a minute?

column9: A cross-country runner keeps a steady, comfortable pace for 40 minutes and can still talk while she runs. Which process makes most of the ATP in her leg muscles?
column14: Lactic acid fermentation
column15: Alcoholic fermentation
column16: Photosynthesis
column17: Aerobic respiration
column28: At a steady pace her heart and lungs deliver enough oxygen, so her muscle cells use aerobic respiration and get about 36 ATP from each glucose. That high yield is what lets her keep going. A common mistake is thinking all exercise is anaerobic; fermentation takes over only when oxygen can't keep up.
column29: If she can talk while running, is she short on oxygen?

column9: Glycolysis has just made pyruvate in a muscle cell that has no oxygen. What happens to the pyruvate next?
column14: It enters the mitochondria for the Krebs cycle, the same as usual
column15: It stays in the cytoplasm and is turned into lactic acid
column16: It is turned into ethanol and carbon dioxide
column17: It is turned back into oxygen
column28: With no oxygen, pyruvate stays in the cytoplasm and lactic acid fermentation turns it into lactic acid. Pyruvate goes into the mitochondria only when oxygen is present. A common mistake is choosing ethanol and carbon dioxide, but that is what yeast make, not animal muscle cells.
column29: No oxygen means no trip into the mitochondria. Which kind of fermentation happens in animals?

column9: Which equation shows aerobic respiration?
column14: C₆H₁₂O₆ → 2C₂H₅OH + 2CO₂ + 2ATP
column15: 6CO₂ + 6H₂O → C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂
column16: C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂ → 6CO₂ + 6H₂O + ATP
column17: C₆H₁₂O₆ → 2C₃H₆O₃ + 2ATP
column28: Aerobic respiration uses glucose and oxygen and makes carbon dioxide, water, and ATP. Choice A is alcoholic fermentation, D is lactic acid fermentation, and B is photosynthesis. A common mistake is choosing B because it has the same molecules; check which side the oxygen is on.
column29: Aerobic means oxygen goes IN. Look for O₂ on the left side of the arrow.

column9: Which process does this equation show? C₆H₁₂O₆ → 2C₃H₆O₃ + 2ATP
column14: Aerobic respiration
column15: Alcoholic fermentation
column16: Lactic acid fermentation
column17: Photosynthesis
column28: C₃H₆O₃ is lactic acid. Glucose is split into 2 lactic acid molecules with a gain of 2 ATP, and no oxygen or carbon dioxide appears. Alcoholic fermentation would show ethanol (C₂H₅OH) and CO₂. A common mistake is calling any equation without oxygen "alcoholic."
column29: Is any oxygen going in or any CO₂ coming out? What molecule is C₃H₆O₃?

column9: A muscle cell can break down the same fuel molecule whether or not oxygen is present. Which molecule is it?
column14: Oxygen
column15: Glucose
column16: Carbon dioxide
column17: Lactic acid
column28: Both kinds of respiration start by breaking down glucose (C₆H₁₂O₆) in glycolysis. Oxygen is used only by aerobic respiration, carbon dioxide is a product, and lactic acid is a waste product of fermentation. A common mistake is choosing oxygen, but oxygen is not broken down for energy.
column29: It's the sugar you get from digesting foods like bread and pasta.

column9: Aerobic respiration, alcoholic fermentation, and lactic acid fermentation all have one product in common. What is it?
column14: Carbon dioxide
column15: Ethanol
column16: ATP
column17: Water
column28: All three make ATP, the cell's energy molecule; they just make different amounts (about 36 vs. 2 per glucose). Carbon dioxide is not made by lactic acid fermentation, ethanol only by alcoholic fermentation, and water only by aerobic respiration. A common mistake is choosing carbon dioxide and forgetting about lactic acid fermentation.
column29: The whole point of respiration is to make this molecule.

column9: Some bacteria live deep in swamp mud where there is no oxygen at all. How do they get energy from their food?
column14: By aerobic respiration in their mitochondria
column15: By anaerobic processes such as fermentation
column16: By pulling oxygen out of the water above
column17: They do not need energy
column28: With no oxygen, these bacteria use anaerobic pathways such as fermentation, which start with glycolysis and need no oxygen. Bacteria have no mitochondria, and the mud has no oxygen to use. A common mistake is thinking every living thing needs oxygen; many microbes don't.
column29: No oxygen is available. Which kind of respiration still works?

column9: Two flasks hold the same yeast and sugar water. Air is bubbled through Flask A. Flask B is sealed so no air can get in, and its oxygen is soon used up. Compared with the yeast in Flask A, the yeast in Flask B get...
column14: more ATP from each glucose
column15: the same ATP from each glucose
column16: much less ATP from each glucose
column17: no ATP at all
column28: Without oxygen, the yeast in Flask B switch to alcoholic fermentation and get only 2 ATP per glucose, compared with about 36 from aerobic respiration in Flask A. They still get some ATP, so "none" is wrong. A common mistake is thinking fermentation makes more because it is faster.
column29: Which flask's yeast can still use their mitochondria?

column9: Glycolysis splits one glucose molecule into two molecules of ___.
column28: Glycolysis breaks 6-carbon glucose into two 3-carbon pyruvate molecules (and nets 2 ATP). What happens to pyruvate next depends on oxygen. A common mistake is writing lactic acid or ethanol, which are made later, during fermentation.
column29: It's a 3-carbon molecule whose name starts with p.

column9: A cell has plenty of glucose but suddenly has no oxygen. What will most likely happen?
column14: It will stop making ATP right away and die
column15: It will make a little ATP using glycolysis and fermentation
column16: It will keep making about 36 ATP per glucose, the same as usual
column17: It will make oxygen out of the glucose it has
column28: Without oxygen, the Krebs cycle and electron transport chain stop, but glycolysis and fermentation still work, giving 2 ATP per glucose. That's why muscles can keep going for a little while when oxygen runs short. A common mistake is thinking the cell instantly runs out of energy.
column29: Which stages don't need oxygen?

column9: Select every product of alcoholic fermentation in yeast. Select all that apply.
column14: Ethanol
column15: Lactic acid
column16: Carbon dioxide
column17: Oxygen
column28: Alcoholic fermentation turns glucose into ethanol, carbon dioxide, and 2 ATP (C₆H₁₂O₆ → 2C₂H₅OH + 2CO₂ + 2ATP). Lactic acid comes from the other kind of fermentation, water only comes from aerobic respiration, and no fermentation makes oxygen. A common mistake is leaving out ATP, which is the whole reason the yeast does it.
column29: Think about what makes bread rise, what gives it an alcohol smell, and why the yeast bothers doing it at all.

column9: Select every product of aerobic respiration. Select all that apply.
column14: Oxygen
column15: Carbon dioxide
column16: Glucose
column17: Water
column28: Aerobic respiration makes carbon dioxide, water, and about 36 ATP per glucose. Glucose and oxygen are the reactants (what goes in), not products. Lactic acid comes only from fermentation. A common mistake is choosing oxygen, which aerobic respiration uses up.
column29: Products are what come OUT of the reaction. Which of these do you breathe out, or does the cell gain?

column9: Select every food that is made with the help of fermentation by microorganisms. Select all that apply.
column14: Yogurt
column15: Fresh-squeezed orange juice
column16: Sourdough bread
column17: Kimchi
column28: Yogurt and kimchi rely on lactic acid bacteria, sourdough uses both yeast and lactic acid bacteria, and soy sauce is fermented by molds, yeast, and bacteria. Fresh juice and raw carrots are not fermented. A common mistake is leaving out bread, but yeast fermentation is what makes bread rise.
column29: Which foods sit with live microbes for hours or days while they are being made?

column9: Put the steps of aerobic respiration in order, starting with the first.
column14: Electron transport chain
column15: Glucose enters the cell
column16: Krebs cycle
column17: Glycolysis
column28: Glucose enters the cell → glycolysis splits it in the cytoplasm → the Krebs cycle runs in the mitochondria → the electron transport chain finishes the job and makes most of the ATP. A common mistake is putting the Krebs cycle first; glucose has to be split by glycolysis before anything goes into the mitochondria.
column29: Glucose gets split in half before the pieces ever go into the mitochondria.

column9: Match each example to the process that is mainly happening.
column14: Cucumbers fermenting in salt brine into sour pickles :: Lactic acid fermentation
column15: Pizza dough rising overnight in the fridge :: Alcoholic fermentation
column16: A sled dog's leg muscles during a steady six-hour run :: Aerobic respiration
column28: Brine pickles are soured by lactic acid bacteria. Yeast in dough make carbon dioxide (and ethanol) by alcoholic fermentation, so the dough rises. A sled dog running at a steady pace for hours gets enough oxygen for aerobic respiration. A common mistake is thinking any long, hard exercise must be anaerobic.
column29: For each one ask: is it bacteria, yeast, or a muscle with a steady oxygen supply?

column9: A yeast cell with no oxygen ferments 10 glucose molecules. How many ATP does it gain in total (net)?
column28: Fermentation nets 2 ATP per glucose, so 10 × 2 = 20 ATP. A common mistake is using 36 ATP per glucose, which only applies when oxygen is present.
column29: How many ATP does fermentation net from ONE glucose? Then multiply.

column9: A liver cell fully breaks down 5 glucose molecules by aerobic respiration. Using 36 ATP per glucose, how many ATP does it make?
column28: 5 × 36 = 180 ATP. If the same 5 glucose were fermented instead, the cell would get only 5 × 2 = 10 ATP. A common mistake is adding (5 + 36) instead of multiplying.
column29: Multiply the number of glucose molecules by the ATP from each one.

column9: Which of these is a kind of anaerobic respiration?
column14: The Krebs cycle
column15: Lactic acid fermentation
column16: The electron transport chain
column17: Photosynthesis
column28: The two kinds of anaerobic respiration are lactic acid fermentation and alcoholic fermentation. The Krebs cycle and electron transport chain are stages of aerobic respiration, and photosynthesis isn't respiration at all. A common mistake is picking the Krebs cycle because it is a step of respiration, but it only keeps running when oxygen is present.
column29: Which choice is a type of fermentation?

column9: In a Venn diagram comparing aerobic respiration and lactic acid fermentation, where does "uses the mitochondria" belong?
column14: Lactic acid fermentation only
column15: In the overlap (both)
column16: Aerobic respiration only
column17: Outside both circles (neither)
column28: Only aerobic respiration uses the mitochondria, for the Krebs cycle and electron transport chain. Lactic acid fermentation happens entirely in the cytoplasm. A common mistake is putting it in the overlap because both start with glycolysis, but glycolysis happens in the cytoplasm, not the mitochondria.
column29: Where in the cell does fermentation happen?

column9: In a Venn diagram comparing aerobic respiration and lactic acid fermentation, where does "releases carbon dioxide" belong?
column14: In the overlap (both)
column15: Lactic acid fermentation only
column16: Aerobic respiration only
column17: Outside both circles (neither)
column28: Aerobic respiration releases CO₂ during the Krebs cycle. Lactic acid fermentation releases no gas at all; all the carbon stays in the lactic acid. A common mistake is putting it in the overlap because alcoholic fermentation releases CO₂, but that is a different type of fermentation.
column29: Does a muscle cell doing lactic acid fermentation give off any gas?

column9: Sourdough bread tastes sour. What causes the sour flavor?
column14: Oxygen made by the yeast
column15: Lactic acid made by bacteria in the starter
column16: Water made by aerobic respiration
column17: Ethanol left over after baking
column28: A sourdough starter holds lactic acid bacteria as well as yeast. The bacteria make lactic acid, which gives the sour taste, while the yeast make the CO₂ that raises the dough. A common mistake is giving the yeast all the credit; the sourness comes from the bacteria.
column29: The name of one type of fermentation has the word acid in it.

column9: When plenty of oxygen is available, where does most of a human cell's ATP come from?
column14: Lactic acid fermentation in the cytoplasm
column15: Aerobic respiration in the mitochondria
column16: Alcoholic fermentation in the nucleus
column17: Photosynthesis in the chloroplasts
column28: With oxygen, cells finish breaking down glucose in the mitochondria and get about 36 ATP per glucose. Fermentation is a backup for when oxygen runs short. Human cells have no chloroplasts and never do alcoholic fermentation. A common mistake is thinking cells ferment all the time.
column29: Aerobic means "with oxygen."

column9: Glycolysis needs oxygen in order to happen.
column28: False. Glycolysis does not need oxygen; that's why it is the first step of BOTH aerobic and anaerobic respiration. Oxygen is needed later, at the end of the electron transport chain. A common mistake is thinking every step of respiration needs oxygen.
column29: Think about which stage yeast in a sealed, airless jar can still run.

column9: Which statement is true about yeast but NOT about human cells?
column14: Yeast make ATP
column15: Yeast break down glucose
column16: Yeast can carry out aerobic respiration
column17: Yeast can make ethanol when they ferment
column28: Yeast do alcoholic fermentation, making ethanol and CO₂. Human cells ferment too, but they make lactic acid instead. Both yeast and human cells make ATP, break down glucose, and can do aerobic respiration. A common mistake is thinking human cells can't do any fermentation.
column29: Three of these are true for both. Which one is only true for yeast?

column9: Which is the best example of aerobic respiration?
column14: Bacteria turning milk into cheese
column15: A goose's flight muscles during a long, steady migration
column16: Yeast making ethanol fuel in a sealed tank at a fuel plant
column17: Bacteria living deep in pond mud where there is no oxygen
column28: Long, steady flight is powered by aerobic respiration because the goose's blood keeps delivering oxygen, giving about 36 ATP per glucose. The other three happen without oxygen and use fermentation or other anaerobic pathways. A common mistake is thinking that hard work like flying must be anaerobic.
column29: Which one has a steady supply of oxygen?

column9: Glycolysis splits one glucose molecule (C₆H₁₂O₆) into two smaller molecules that each have the same number of carbon atoms. How many carbon atoms does each one have?
column28: Glucose has 6 carbons, and glycolysis splits it into two equal 3-carbon molecules (pyruvate): 6 ÷ 2 = 3. A common mistake is answering 6 or 2 by not dividing the carbons evenly.
column29: Count the carbons in C₆H₁₂O₆, then split them evenly in two.

column9: Which stage of aerobic respiration makes most of the ATP?
column14: Glycolysis
column15: Krebs cycle
column16: Electron transport chain
column17: Fermentation
column28: The electron transport chain makes about 32 to 34 ATP per glucose; glycolysis and the Krebs cycle make only 2 each. That's why losing oxygen, which the electron transport chain needs, cuts the ATP so much. A common mistake is choosing the Krebs cycle because it is the best-known stage.
column29: It's the last stage, on the inner membrane of the mitochondria.

column9: Cheese makers add bacteria to milk. The bacteria turn milk sugar into lactic acid, which helps the milk curdle. What kind of respiration are the bacteria doing?
column14: Lactic acid fermentation
column15: Aerobic respiration
column16: Alcoholic fermentation
column17: Photosynthesis
column28: Making lactic acid from sugar is lactic acid fermentation, a type of anaerobic respiration. Aerobic respiration would make carbon dioxide and water, and alcoholic fermentation would make ethanol. A common mistake is choosing alcoholic fermentation just because it's a food-making process.
column29: Look at the product the bacteria make. Which process is named after it?

column9: About how many times more ATP does aerobic respiration make from one glucose molecule than fermentation does?
column28: Aerobic respiration makes about 36 ATP per glucose and fermentation makes 2, so 36 ÷ 2 = 18 times more. (Any answer from 15 to 19 is accepted, since books give slightly different aerobic totals.) A common mistake is subtracting (36 − 2 = 34) instead of dividing.
column29: "How many times more" means divide the bigger ATP number by the smaller one.

column9: A muscle cell ferments 5 glucose molecules by lactic acid fermentation. How many lactic acid molecules does it make?
column28: Each glucose (6 carbons) splits into 2 lactic acid molecules (3 carbons each): C₆H₁₂O₆ → 2C₃H₆O₃ + 2ATP. So 5 × 2 = 10. A common mistake is answering 5, forgetting that each glucose gives two.
column29: How many 3-carbon pieces come from one 6-carbon glucose?

column9: A mouse fully breaks down 4 glucose molecules by aerobic respiration. How many CO₂ molecules does it release?
column28: Aerobic respiration takes glucose all the way apart, so each glucose releases 6 CO₂ (C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂ → 6CO₂ + 6H₂O). 4 × 6 = 24. A common mistake is using 2 CO₂ per glucose, which is the amount from alcoholic fermentation.
column29: Each glucose has 6 carbons, and each CO₂ carries away one of them.

column9: Look at this reaction: C₆H₁₂O₆ → 2C₂H₅OH + 2CO₂ + 2ATP. How many carbon atoms are on the product side (count ethanol and CO₂)?
column28: 2 ethanol × 2 carbons = 4, plus 2 CO₂ × 1 carbon = 2, for 6 total, the same 6 carbons that were in glucose. Atoms are rearranged, not destroyed. A common mistake is forgetting to multiply by the 2 in front of each formula.
column29: Multiply each formula's carbons by the big number in front of it, then add.

column9: When comparing alcoholic fermentation with aerobic respiration, which feature belongs ONLY in the alcoholic fermentation circle?
column14: Releases carbon dioxide
column15: Makes ethanol
column16: Makes ATP
column17: Starts with glycolysis
column28: Only alcoholic fermentation makes ethanol. Both processes release carbon dioxide, make ATP, and start with glycolysis, so those go in the overlap. A common mistake is putting "releases carbon dioxide" under fermentation only, forgetting that aerobic respiration releases CO₂ in the Krebs cycle.
column29: Three of these are true for BOTH processes.

column9: Select every feature that aerobic respiration and lactic acid fermentation have in common. Select all that apply.
column14: Both start with glycolysis
column15: Both need oxygen
column16: Both break down glucose
column17: Both release carbon dioxide
column28: Both start with glycolysis, both break down glucose, and both make ATP (about 36 vs. 2). Only aerobic respiration needs oxygen, releases CO₂, and uses the mitochondria. A common mistake is choosing "release carbon dioxide," which is true for alcoholic fermentation but not lactic acid fermentation.
column29: Test each choice on a muscle cell that is completely out of oxygen.

column9: Flask A holds yeast in sugar water. Flask B holds bacteria that carry out lactic acid fermentation in sugar water. Both flasks are sealed with no oxygen and have a balloon on top. After an hour, Flask A's balloon has inflated but Flask B's has not. What is the best explanation?
column14: Alcoholic fermentation releases CO₂ gas, but lactic acid fermentation does not
column15: The bacteria in Flask B must have died before making anything
column16: The yeast in Flask A made oxygen gas that filled the balloon
column17: Lactic acid fermentation makes no ATP at all, so the bacteria quickly stopped working
column28: Yeast do alcoholic fermentation, which releases CO₂ that fills the balloon. Lactic acid fermentation keeps all the carbon in lactic acid, so no gas forms even though the bacteria are alive and making ATP. A common mistake is assuming the bacteria died because nothing visible happened.
column29: Compare the products of the two kinds of fermentation. Which one includes a gas?

column9: Jar A has yeast and sugar water with air pumped through it. Jar B has the same yeast and sugar water but is sealed with no air. After two hours, which result is most likely?
column14: Jar B has many more yeast cells, and Jar A smells like alcohol
column15: Both jars have the same number of yeast cells and the same smell
column16: Neither jar's yeast are making any ATP
column17: Jar A has many more yeast cells, and Jar B smells like alcohol
column28: With oxygen, the yeast in Jar A use aerobic respiration and get about 36 ATP per glucose, so they have lots of energy to grow and divide. The yeast in Jar B ferment, getting only 2 ATP per glucose and making ethanol, which gives the alcohol smell. A common mistake is switching the jars around.
column29: Which jar's yeast get more energy from the same sugar? Which jar's yeast make ethanol?

column9: In the Muscle Fatigue Lab, a student squeezes a clothespin as many times as possible in four back-to-back 30-second trials with no rest. The counts are 58, 49, 41, and 35. What best explains the drop?
column14: The hand muscles completely ran out of glucose after the first 30 seconds, so they had no fuel left
column15: The hand muscles switched to alcoholic fermentation and made ethanol
column16: Oxygen couldn't keep up, so the muscles leaned on lactic acid fermentation, which makes less ATP
column17: The hand muscles made more ATP each trial, so they needed fewer squeezes
column28: Fast, repeated squeezing uses ATP faster than blood can bring oxygen, so muscle cells lean on lactic acid fermentation. It makes only 2 ATP per glucose and lets lactic acid build up, so the muscles tire and the count drops. A common mistake is saying the muscles ran out of glucose, but they still have sugar; they are short on oxygen.
column29: What is the hand short on: glucose or oxygen?

column9: After a 200-meter sprint, you keep breathing hard for several minutes even though you are standing still. Why?
column14: You are breathing out ethanol that your muscle cells made during the sprint, to clear it from your blood
column15: Your lungs switched to fermentation and need extra air to stop it
column16: Your muscle cells made extra oxygen during the sprint and must now release it through your lungs
column17: You are taking in extra oxygen so cells can return to aerobic respiration and clear lactic acid
column28: During the sprint your muscles used lactic acid fermentation because oxygen couldn't keep up. Afterward, the extra oxygen you breathe in lets cells return to aerobic respiration and deal with the lactic acid. A common mistake is saying muscles make ethanol; human cells make lactic acid, not alcohol.
column29: What did your muscles run short of during the sprint?

column9: Which of these could stay alive for a whole day in a sealed jar of sugar water with no oxygen, making all of its ATP by fermentation?
column14: A hamster
column15: Baker's yeast
column16: A sparrow
column17: A kitten
column28: Yeast can live on alcoholic fermentation alone, even though it gives only 2 ATP per glucose. Mammals and birds need far more ATP for their whole bodies than fermentation can supply, so they depend on aerobic respiration; their muscles can ferment only for short bursts. A common mistake is thinking any animal can switch to fermentation for a long time.
column29: Which organism is used to ferment bread dough?

column9: Why can't your leg muscles run on lactic acid fermentation for a whole hour of hard exercise?
column14: It uses up oxygen faster than the lungs can supply it
column15: It releases too much carbon dioxide into the blood
column16: It gives little ATP per glucose, and lactic acid builds up, so muscles tire
column17: It happens inside the mitochondria, which wear out and stop working after a while
column28: Lactic acid fermentation makes ATP fast but only 2 per glucose, and lactic acid builds up in the muscle, so you can't keep it up. It uses no oxygen, releases no CO₂, and happens in the cytoplasm. A common mistake is choosing the oxygen answer; fermentation is what happens when oxygen is short.
column29: Think about both the amount of ATP and what builds up in the muscle.

column9: Which cell in your body would you expect to have the most mitochondria?
column14: A mature red blood cell
column15: A dead skin cell on the surface
column16: A heart muscle cell that beats nonstop
column17: A fat-storage cell
column28: Heart muscle works every second of your life and depends on aerobic respiration for its huge, steady ATP needs, so its cells are packed with mitochondria. Mature red blood cells have no mitochondria at all, and skin and fat cells use much less energy. A common mistake is choosing red blood cells because they carry oxygen; carrying oxygen is not the same as using it.
column29: Which cell needs the most ATP, all day, every day?

column9: Put these molecules in order from MOST carbon atoms to FEWEST.
column14: Ethanol (C₂H₅OH)
column15: Glucose (C₆H₁₂O₆)
column16: Carbon dioxide (CO₂)
column17: Lactic acid (C₃H₆O₃)
column28: Glucose has 6 carbons, lactic acid 3, ethanol 2, and CO₂ 1. That's why one glucose can become two lactic acids (3 + 3), or two ethanols plus two CO₂ (2 + 2 + 1 + 1). A common mistake is counting hydrogens or oxygens instead of only the C's.
column29: Count only the number after each C (no number means 1).

column9: Mature human red blood cells have no mitochondria. How do they make ATP?
column14: Glycolysis followed by lactic acid fermentation
column15: The Krebs cycle in their cytoplasm
column16: The electron transport chain on their cell membrane
column17: Glycolysis followed by alcoholic fermentation
column28: Without mitochondria, red blood cells can't run the Krebs cycle or electron transport chain, so they use glycolysis and lactic acid fermentation in the cytoplasm. Human cells never do alcoholic fermentation. A common mistake is thinking that because red blood cells carry oxygen, they must use aerobic respiration.
column29: Which steps can happen without mitochondria? Which kind of fermentation do human cells use?

column9: A student says, "Anaerobic respiration is just aerobic respiration that happens faster." What is the best correction?
column14: Anaerobic respiration actually uses more oxygen than aerobic respiration does
column15: It uses the same steps in the mitochondria as aerobic respiration, just running at a faster speed
column16: The student is correct; the two processes differ only in speed
column17: They share only glycolysis; anaerobic skips the Krebs cycle and ETC and makes far less ATP
column28: The two processes share only glycolysis. After that, aerobic respiration uses oxygen in the mitochondria (Krebs cycle and electron transport chain), while anaerobic respiration uses fermentation in the cytoplasm and nets just 2 ATP. It is faster, but it is not the same process. A common mistake is agreeing because anaerobic respiration really is faster.
column29: Which stages does each process actually use after glycolysis?

column9: Select every process or stage that releases carbon dioxide. Select all that apply.
column14: Glycolysis
column15: The Krebs cycle
column16: Alcoholic fermentation
column17: Lactic acid fermentation
column28: The Krebs cycle releases CO₂, so aerobic respiration as a whole does too. Alcoholic fermentation releases 2 CO₂ per glucose. Glycolysis releases no CO₂ (it only splits glucose in half), and lactic acid fermentation releases none either. A common mistake is picking glycolysis because it is the step that breaks glucose apart.
column29: Track the carbons: in which steps does a carbon leave as a gas?

column9: Yogurt stays good in the refrigerator much longer than fresh milk. How does lactic acid fermentation help?
column14: The fermentation adds oxygen to the milk, which kills all of the bacteria in it
column15: The fermentation turns milk sugar into ethanol, which preserves it
column16: The fermentation removes all of the water from the milk so nothing can grow in it
column17: The lactic acid makes yogurt acidic, which slows the microbes that spoil food
column28: The bacteria turn milk sugar into lactic acid, and the acid lowers the pH so most spoilage microbes can't grow well. Fermentation doesn't add oxygen, make ethanol (that's yeast), or dry the food out. A common mistake is thinking all fermentation preserves food with alcohol.
column29: What does the name lactic ACID tell you about the yogurt?

column9: Why does the electron transport chain stop when a cell runs out of oxygen?
column14: Oxygen is the fuel that the chain burns to release energy, the way a fire burns wood
column15: Oxygen carries glucose into the mitochondria for the chain
column16: The chain uses oxygen as a building block to make glucose
column17: Oxygen must be at the end of the chain to accept the electrons (forming water)
column28: NADH and FADH₂ bring electrons to the chain, and oxygen waits at the very end to pick them up, combining with hydrogen to form water. With no oxygen, electrons back up and the chain stops, so the cell is left with fermentation. A common mistake is calling oxygen the fuel; glucose is the fuel.
column29: Think of the chain as a line of people passing something along. Who is at the very end to take it?

column9: After days of heavy rain, a corn field floods and the soil fills with water, leaving almost no oxygen around the roots. What happens in the root cells?
column14: They switch to fermentation and get much less ATP, which can damage the roots
column15: They switch to photosynthesis to make their own oxygen underground, using the extra water
column16: They make more ATP than usual because there is extra water
column17: They split the water molecules in the soil to get the oxygen they need for respiration
column28: Plant cells do aerobic respiration too. When flooding cuts off oxygen, root cells fall back on fermentation, which gives only 2 ATP per glucose, so the roots weaken if it lasts. Roots are in the dark and can't photosynthesize. A common mistake is thinking plants don't do respiration because they photosynthesize.
column29: Roots are underground with no light. What happens to any cell that loses its oxygen supply?

column9: Yeast are sealed in a flask with sugar water, and sensors record the oxygen and ethanol. At 0 min: oxygen 20%, ethanol none. At 30 min: oxygen 9%, ethanol none. At 60 min: oxygen 0%, ethanol a trace. At 90 min: oxygen 0%, ethanol rising. What is the best conclusion?
column14: The yeast made oxygen during the first hour of the experiment
column15: The yeast did alcoholic fermentation for the entire 90 minutes
column16: Aerobic respiration until the oxygen ran out, then fermentation
column17: The yeast all died at 60 minutes, when the oxygen hit 0%
column28: Oxygen dropped while no ethanol formed, which means aerobic respiration. Once oxygen hit 0%, ethanol began to build up, which is the sign of alcoholic fermentation. If the yeast had died, ethanol would not keep rising. A common mistake is ignoring the time when ethanol first appears.
column29: When did ethanol start showing up, and what had just happened to the oxygen?

column9: A sensor shows that an unknown microbe in a jar is releasing CO₂. Which extra measurement would best tell you whether it is doing aerobic respiration or alcoholic fermentation?
column14: The color of the liquid inside the jar
column15: Whether the jar's CO₂ level keeps on rising
column16: Whether oxygen is used up and whether ethanol forms
column17: How much the jar and its lid weigh
column28: Both aerobic respiration and alcoholic fermentation release CO₂, so CO₂ alone can't tell them apart. Aerobic respiration uses up oxygen; alcoholic fermentation makes ethanol and uses no oxygen. A common mistake is choosing the CO₂ reading, which you already know is rising.
column29: What does one process use up and the other one make that the other doesn't?

column9: Select every cell or organism that carries out lactic acid fermentation. Select all that apply.
column14: Human leg muscle cells during an all-out sprint
column15: Baker's yeast in bread dough
column16: Bacteria that turn milk into yogurt
column17: Bacteria that ferment cabbage into sauerkraut
column18: Yeast making ethanol fuel from corn
column28: Human muscle cells, yogurt bacteria, and sauerkraut bacteria all make lactic acid. Yeast, in bread or in ethanol plants, do alcoholic fermentation instead. A common mistake is thinking yeast make lactic acid because they're used in food too.
column29: Sort them: which ones are yeast and which are bacteria or muscle cells?

column9: Using 36 ATP per glucose, a cell made 108 ATP by aerobic respiration. How many glucose molecules did it use?
column28: 108 ÷ 36 = 3 glucose molecules. Fermenting those same 3 glucose would have given only 3 × 2 = 6 ATP. A common mistake is multiplying (108 × 36) instead of dividing.
column29: Divide the total ATP by the ATP from one glucose.

column9: A muscle cell made 14 ATP by fermentation alone. How many glucose molecules did it ferment?
column28: Fermentation nets 2 ATP per glucose, so 14 ÷ 2 = 7 glucose. A common mistake is dividing by 36, which is the aerobic number.
column29: How many ATP does one fermented glucose give? Divide by that.

column9: Which choice correctly describes where each process happens in a yeast cell?
column14: Aerobic respiration happens entirely in the cytoplasm; fermentation starts in the cytoplasm and finishes in the mitochondria
column15: Both start in the cytoplasm and finish in the mitochondria; fermentation just goes faster
column16: Aerobic respiration happens in the nucleus; fermentation happens entirely in the cytoplasm
column17: Aerobic respiration starts in the cytoplasm and finishes in the mitochondria; fermentation happens entirely in the cytoplasm
column28: Glycolysis (step one of both) is in the cytoplasm. Aerobic respiration then moves into the mitochondria for the Krebs cycle and electron transport chain. Fermentation never leaves the cytoplasm. A common mistake is saying all of aerobic respiration happens in the mitochondria and forgetting glycolysis.
column29: Where does glycolysis happen, and which process goes on into the mitochondria afterward?

column9: A student adds yogurt bacteria (which carry out lactic acid fermentation) to bread dough instead of yeast. Will the dough rise like normal?
column14: Yes, because every kind of fermentation makes gas
column15: Yes, because lactic acid is a gas that fills the dough
column16: No, because bacteria can't break down any sugar
column17: No, because lactic acid fermentation makes no CO₂ gas
column28: Dough rises from trapped CO₂ gas. Yogurt bacteria make lactic acid, which is not a gas, so this dough won't rise like yeast dough (though it might taste sour). The bacteria can break down sugar; they just make a different product. A common mistake is thinking every kind of fermentation makes bubbles.
column29: Which product actually lifts bread dough, and does lactic acid fermentation make it?

column9: Endurance training can increase the number of mitochondria in muscle cells. How would this most likely help a runner in a long race?
column14: Her muscles will make more lactic acid, giving her more energy late in the race
column15: Her muscles will switch to alcoholic fermentation, which is faster
column16: Her muscles will need no glucose, because mitochondria make their own
column17: More ATP comes from aerobic respiration, so she relies less on fermentation
column28: More mitochondria means more places to run the Krebs cycle and electron transport chain, so muscles get more ATP aerobically (about 36 per glucose) and need less fermentation. Mitochondria use glucose; they don't make it. A common mistake is thinking more mitochondria means more lactic acid.
column29: Which process happens in mitochondria?

column9: Scientists study a yeast strain whose mitochondria don't work, though the cells stay alive. If these yeast are given sugar and plenty of oxygen, how can they make ATP?
column14: By aerobic respiration as usual, getting about 36 ATP per glucose
column15: They can't make any ATP at all
column16: Only by glycolysis and fermentation, getting 2 ATP per glucose
column17: By photosynthesis
column28: Oxygen alone isn't enough; the Krebs cycle and electron transport chain happen in the mitochondria. Without working mitochondria, these yeast can only use glycolysis and fermentation in the cytoplasm. A common mistake is thinking that having oxygen automatically means aerobic respiration.
column29: Where do the oxygen-using stages happen?

column9: To make sauerkraut, cabbage is packed under salty brine so air can't reach it. Why does keeping the air out matter?
column14: Lactic acid bacteria can ferment it, while air-needing molds can't grow
column15: It lets yeast make ethanol inside the cabbage leaves
column16: It traps carbon dioxide so the cabbage puffs up and rises like bread dough
column17: It lets the cabbage keep doing photosynthesis in the jar
column28: With no oxygen, lactic acid bacteria can thrive by fermentation, and the acid they make protects the cabbage. Molds that spoil food need oxygen, so keeping air out keeps them from growing. A common mistake is thinking the bacteria need oxygen to make sauerkraut.
column29: Which microbes need oxygen, and which can live without it?

column9: Yeast need a steady supply of ATP to stay alive. When their oxygen runs out and they switch to fermentation, how must their use of glucose change to keep making the same amount of ATP each minute?
column14: They must use glucose about 2 times faster
column15: They can use glucose more slowly, because fermentation is more efficient
column16: Their glucose use doesn't change
column17: They must use glucose about 18 times faster
column28: Aerobic respiration gives about 36 ATP per glucose and fermentation gives 2, so 36 ÷ 2 = 18 times as much glucose is needed for the same ATP. That's why fermenting yeast go through sugar so fast. A common mistake is choosing "2 times" by using the 2 ATP number directly.
column29: Compare the ATP per glucose. How many fermented glucose equal one aerobic glucose?

column9: A yeast cell needs 360 ATP. How many glucose molecules must it break down to get that much if it is fermenting with no oxygen?
column28: Fermentation nets 2 ATP per glucose, so 360 ÷ 2 = 180 glucose. With oxygen it would need only 360 ÷ 36 = 10. A common mistake is dividing by 36 even though there is no oxygen.
column29: No oxygen means which ATP-per-glucose number?

column9: A muscle cell breaks down 10 glucose molecules: 6 by aerobic respiration and 4 by lactic acid fermentation. Using 36 ATP per glucose for aerobic respiration, how many ATP does it make in total?
column28: Aerobic: 6 × 36 = 216 ATP. Fermentation: 4 × 2 = 8 ATP. Total: 216 + 8 = 224 ATP. A common mistake is using 36 for all 10 glucose (360) or forgetting to add the fermentation ATP.
column29: Work out each part separately, then add them.

column9: Fermentation's ATP per glucose is what percent of aerobic respiration's? Use 36 ATP per glucose for aerobic respiration, and round to the nearest tenth of a percent.
column28: 2 ÷ 36 = 0.0556, and 0.0556 × 100 = 5.6%. Fermentation gets only about one-eighteenth of the ATP. A common mistake is dividing 36 by 2 (which gives 18, the "times more" answer) instead of 2 by 36.
column29: Percent = part ÷ whole × 100. Which number is the part?

column9: Yeast in a sealed flask with no oxygen release 30 CO₂ molecules by alcoholic fermentation. How many glucose molecules did they ferment?
column28: Alcoholic fermentation releases 2 CO₂ per glucose (C₆H₁₂O₆ → 2C₂H₅OH + 2CO₂ + 2ATP), so 30 ÷ 2 = 15 glucose. A common mistake is dividing by 6, which is the CO₂ per glucose for aerobic respiration.
column29: How many CO₂ does fermentation release from one glucose?

column9: E. coli bacteria have no mitochondria, yet they can carry out aerobic respiration. How is that possible?
column14: They borrow mitochondria from the human gut cells that surround them
column15: They use chloroplasts, which do the same job as mitochondria
column16: They can't; any cell without mitochondria can only do fermentation
column17: The steps happen in their cytoplasm and on their cell membrane
column28: Bacteria are prokaryotes with no membrane-bound organelles, so their aerobic steps happen in the cytoplasm and on the cell membrane. In eukaryotes like us, those same steps are in the mitochondria. A common mistake is thinking aerobic respiration is impossible without mitochondria.
column29: Prokaryotes still have a membrane around the whole cell. Where could the electron transport chain sit?

column9: The 2 ATP from fermentation all come from glycolysis; the fermentation step itself makes no extra ATP. So what does the fermentation step do for the cell?
column14: It unloads electrons from NADH, freeing NAD⁺ so glycolysis can keep making ATP
column15: It makes oxygen so the electron transport chain can restart
column16: It turns pyruvate back into glucose so the cell can reuse it
column17: It makes about 34 extra ATP in the cytoplasm, so the cell doesn't need oxygen at all
column28: Glycolysis loads electrons onto NAD⁺, making NADH. Without oxygen, the electron transport chain can't unload NADH, so the cell runs out of empty carriers and glycolysis would stop. Fermentation passes those electrons to pyruvate (making lactic acid or ethanol), freeing NAD⁺ so glycolysis keeps making 2 ATP. A common mistake is thinking fermentation itself makes the ATP.
column29: Glycolysis needs an empty electron carrier to keep going. Without oxygen, what empties it?

column9: Ethanol made by yeast can be burned as fuel in car engines. What does this tell you about alcoholic fermentation?
column14: Much of glucose's energy is still stored in the ethanol
column15: Fermentation releases more energy than aerobic respiration does
column16: Ethanol is a type of ATP that car engines can use directly
column17: Fermentation destroys most of the energy stored in glucose
column28: If ethanol can still be burned for energy, then the yeast left most of glucose's energy locked in it. That explains why fermentation gets only 2 ATP while aerobic respiration, which breaks glucose all the way to CO₂ and water, gets about 36. Energy is not destroyed. A common mistake is thinking fermentation wastes energy by destroying it.
column29: If a molecule can be burned as fuel, does it still have energy in it?

column9: A cheetah chasing a gazelle needs a huge amount of ATP in just a few seconds. Why is anaerobic respiration useful here even though it gets so little ATP from each glucose?
column14: It makes more ATP per glucose than aerobic respiration does, so less fuel is needed
column15: It lets the muscles skip glucose and burn oxygen instead for faster energy
column16: It makes extra oxygen for the muscles during the chase
column17: It makes ATP very quickly, without waiting for more oxygen to arrive
column28: In a burst, muscles need ATP faster than the heart and lungs can deliver oxygen. Glycolysis and fermentation are fast and need no oxygen, so they fill the gap, though the cheetah can only keep it up for a short time. A common mistake is thinking anaerobic respiration is useful because it is efficient; it's useful because it is fast.
column29: What is the limit in a sprint: the amount of glucose or how fast oxygen arrives?

column9: A student wants to test whether yeast release CO₂ when there is no oxygen. Which setup is the best experiment?
column14: One flask of yeast and sugar water left open to the air, with a balloon on top
column15: Two flasks of yeast and sugar water open to the air, one at 10 °C and one at 35 °C
column16: Two sealed, oxygen-free flasks of sugar water with balloons; one gets more yeast and also more sugar than the other
column17: Two sealed, oxygen-free flasks of sugar water at the same temperature with balloons; only one gets yeast
column28: The best design keeps oxygen out of both flasks and changes only one thing (yeast or no yeast), so any gas in the yeast flask must come from the yeast fermenting. The open flasks let oxygen in, so they can't test life without oxygen, and changing yeast and sugar together makes the result impossible to explain. A common mistake is choosing a setup with no control.
column29: A good experiment changes only one variable and has a control. Which setup does that with no oxygen?

column9: Select every statement that correctly contrasts aerobic and anaerobic respiration. Select all that apply.
column14: Only aerobic respiration uses the Krebs cycle and electron transport chain
column15: Aerobic respiration makes about 36 ATP per glucose; anaerobic respiration makes 2
column16: Only aerobic respiration makes water
column17: Only anaerobic respiration begins with glycolysis
column18: Anaerobic respiration happens in the mitochondria
column28: Only aerobic respiration runs the Krebs cycle and electron transport chain, makes water, and gets about 36 ATP. Both begin with glycolysis, anaerobic respiration happens in the cytoplasm, and anaerobic respiration is the faster one. A common mistake is choosing "aerobic is faster" because it makes more ATP; more is not the same as faster.
column29: Check each statement carefully; one word like "only" or "faster" can make it false.

column9: Cyanide is a poison that blocks the electron transport chain. Why is it so deadly to humans, even though cells can still do glycolysis?
column14: Cells get only about 2 ATP per glucose, too little for heart and brain
column15: Cyanide makes cells produce so much ATP that they swell up and burst open
column16: Cyanide turns the glucose inside cells into oxygen gas
column17: Cyanide makes human cells start carrying out photosynthesis instead of respiration
column28: The electron transport chain makes most of the ATP in aerobic respiration. With it blocked, cells are left with glycolysis and fermentation, only 2 ATP per glucose, and the heart and brain can't survive on that. A common mistake is thinking glycolysis alone can keep a person alive.
column29: Which stage makes most of the ATP, and how much is left without it?

column9: Match each lab observation to the conclusion it best supports.
column14: A sealed flask's balloon inflates, and the liquid smells like alcohol :: Alcoholic fermentation is happening
column15: Yeast grow and divide quickly in a flask with air bubbling through it :: Aerobic respiration is happening
column16: Milk turns sour and thick, but no gas bubbles form :: Lactic acid fermentation is happening
column28: Gas plus an alcohol smell means ethanol and CO₂, the products of alcoholic fermentation. Fast growth with air means lots of ATP from aerobic respiration. Sour milk with no gas means lactic acid with no CO₂, which is lactic acid fermentation. A common mistake is matching any bubbles to aerobic respiration.
column29: Look for clues: alcohol smell, sour taste, gas or no gas, oxygen or no oxygen.

column9: Match each organism or cell to the description that fits it.
column14: Clostridium botulinum (bacteria that can grow in badly sealed cans) :: Grows only where there is no oxygen
column15: Baker's yeast :: Can switch between aerobic respiration and fermentation
column16: A human brain cell :: Needs a steady oxygen supply because it depends on aerobic respiration
column28: Clostridium botulinum is poisoned by oxygen, which is why it can grow in sealed, airless cans. Yeast use aerobic respiration with oxygen and switch to alcoholic fermentation without it. Brain cells use a lot of ATP and can't survive long without oxygen. A common mistake is thinking every cell can live on fermentation if it has to.
column29: Which one lives in airless places, which one is flexible, and which one is in trouble within minutes without oxygen?

column9: Lactic acid is C₃H₆O₃ and glucose is C₆H₁₂O₆. Why does lactic acid fermentation release no CO₂?
column14: Glucose's 6 carbons all end up in the two 3-carbon lactic acids
column15: Lactic acid fermentation uses up CO₂ as one of its reactants, so none is left over
column16: The CO₂ is stored inside the ATP molecules that are made
column17: The muscles breathe out the CO₂ before it can be measured
column28: One glucose (6 C) becomes two lactic acids (3 C + 3 C = 6 C). Every carbon is accounted for, so none leaves as CO₂. In alcoholic fermentation, each 3-carbon piece loses one carbon as CO₂, leaving 2-carbon ethanol. A common mistake is thinking all respiration must release CO₂.
column29: Count the carbons on each side: 6 in, how many in two lactic acids?

column9: Hummingbird flight muscles are packed with mitochondria. Chicken breast muscle (white meat) has far fewer, and chickens fly only in short bursts. What is the best conclusion?
column14: Hummingbird muscle relies mostly on aerobic respiration, and chicken breast more on anaerobic respiration
column15: Chicken breast muscle relies more on aerobic respiration than hummingbird flight muscle does, so it tires less
column16: Both muscles rely only on fermentation, so the number of mitochondria doesn't matter
column17: Mitochondria make glucose, so hummingbirds need to eat less food than chickens
column28: Lots of mitochondria means lots of aerobic respiration, which supports long, steady activity like hovering and migrating. Few mitochondria fit muscles built for quick bursts powered by glycolysis and fermentation. A common mistake is thinking mitochondria make food; they break it down.
column29: What does a large number of mitochondria tell you about which process a muscle uses most?

column9: A muscle cell got 72 ATP from aerobic respiration and 8 ATP from lactic acid fermentation. Using 36 ATP per glucose for aerobic respiration, how many glucose molecules did it use in all?
column28: Aerobic: 72 ÷ 36 = 2 glucose. Fermentation: 8 ÷ 2 = 4 glucose. Total: 2 + 4 = 6 glucose. A common mistake is dividing the total 80 ATP by 36, which ignores that fermentation gets much less ATP per glucose.
column29: Find the glucose for each process separately, then add.

column9: In a lab, a runner's blood lactic acid stays low as her speed goes from walking to an easy jog, then climbs steeply once she runs faster than about 12 km/h. Which explanation fits best?
column14: Her muscles need ATP faster than oxygen arrives, so they add lactic acid fermentation
column15: Above that speed, her muscles stop doing glycolysis completely
column16: Above that speed, her lungs start breathing in lactic acid from the air around the track
column17: Above that speed, her muscles switch to alcoholic fermentation instead
column28: At low speeds, oxygen delivery keeps up and aerobic respiration supplies the ATP, so little lactic acid forms. Past a certain speed, demand outruns oxygen supply and fermentation adds fast ATP, so lactic acid climbs. Glycolysis keeps running the whole time, and human muscles never do alcoholic fermentation. A common mistake is thinking lactic acid comes from the air.
column29: What changes at higher speeds: the need for ATP, the oxygen supply, or both?

column9: Put the steps of an experiment comparing how much gas yeast make with and without oxygen in order.
column14: Measure each balloon's size every 10 minutes
column15: Write a hypothesis about which flask will make more gas
column16: Set up two flasks with the same yeast, sugar water, and temperature, and remove the oxygen from one
column17: Compare the results to the hypothesis and draw a conclusion
column18: Put a balloon over the top of each flask
column28: Hypothesis → set up matched flasks (only oxygen differs) → put on balloons to catch gas → measure over time → compare to the hypothesis. A common mistake is measuring before the balloons are on, or writing the hypothesis after seeing the results.
column29: A hypothesis comes before the experiment, and the conclusion comes last.

column9: Glycolysis happens in the cytoplasm of almost every living thing and needs no oxygen. Early Earth's atmosphere had almost no oxygen. Which conclusion do these facts best support?
column14: Anaerobic pathways like glycolysis probably evolved first
column15: Aerobic respiration probably evolved before glycolysis
column16: Glycolysis probably evolved after mitochondria did
column17: Early life on Earth probably did not need energy
column28: If early Earth had little oxygen, the first cells had to make ATP without it, and glycolysis, which almost all organisms share and which needs no oxygen, fits that. Aerobic respiration could only take off once oxygen was available. A common mistake is assuming the more efficient process must be older.
column29: Which process could work on a planet with almost no oxygen?

column9: Two batches of yeast each break down 100 glucose molecules. The yeast in an aerated tank use only aerobic respiration. The yeast in a sealed bowl of dough use only alcoholic fermentation. How does the CO₂ they release compare?
column14: The sealed yeast release more CO₂, since fermentation is what makes bread rise
column15: The aerated yeast release about 3 times as much CO₂
column16: They release the same amount of CO₂
column17: Only the sealed yeast release CO₂
column28: Aerobic respiration releases 6 CO₂ per glucose (600 total), while alcoholic fermentation releases 2 per glucose (200 total). 600 ÷ 200 = 3. Bread rises from fermentation because dough is airless, not because fermentation makes more gas. A common mistake is thinking only fermentation makes CO₂.
column29: Compare CO₂ per glucose in each process, then multiply by 100.

column9: A student discovers a new single-celled organism. Select every observation that is evidence it can get energy (make ATP) WITHOUT oxygen. Select all that apply.
column14: It keeps making ATP and dividing in a sealed jar after all the oxygen is gone
column15: It releases ethanol in a jar with no oxygen
column16: It uses up oxygen when it is in an open dish
column17: It has mitochondria
column18: It makes lactic acid in a jar with no oxygen
column28: Growing, making ethanol, or making lactic acid after all oxygen is gone all show the organism can run on anaerobic pathways. Using oxygen in an open dish only shows it CAN do aerobic respiration, and having mitochondria doesn't rule out fermentation (yeast have both). A common mistake is choosing the oxygen-use observation.
column29: Which observations were made with NO oxygen present?

column9: A mutant yeast strain has a broken fermentation step but normal glycolysis. In a sealed jar with no oxygen, what happens to it?
column14: Glycolysis stops because NADH can't be recycled to NAD⁺, so ATP production stops
column15: It switches to aerobic respiration and makes about 36 ATP per glucose instead of 2
column16: It makes extra CO₂ because its glycolysis speeds up to make up for it
column17: Nothing changes, because the fermentation step never makes any ATP of its own anyway
column28: Glycolysis needs NAD⁺ to keep going. Without oxygen (no electron transport chain) and without fermentation, there is no way to unload NADH, so NAD⁺ runs out, glycolysis stops, and ATP production stops. A common mistake is choosing "nothing changes" because fermentation itself doesn't make ATP; it still keeps glycolysis running.
column29: What does glycolysis need a steady supply of, and which step normally recycles it when there is no oxygen?

column9: Leaves that fall into a waterlogged bog with almost no oxygen break down much more slowly than leaves on a dry forest floor. Which explanation fits best?
column14: Without oxygen, decomposers get far less ATP, so decay is slow
column15: Bog water holds extra oxygen that protects the leaves from decay
column16: The leaves keep doing photosynthesis under the bog water
column17: Anaerobic decomposers get more ATP per glucose than aerobic ones do
column28: Decomposers on the forest floor get about 36 ATP per glucose from aerobic respiration, giving them plenty of energy to grow and digest leaves. In the airless bog, microbes are limited to anaerobic pathways with far less ATP, so decay is slow. A common mistake is thinking anaerobic microbes are more powerful because they can live without oxygen.
column29: How much ATP can a decomposer get per glucose with and without oxygen?

column9: Goldfish can survive for days with no oxygen in a pond frozen over with ice. Their muscle cells turn pyruvate into ethanol, which passes out through the gills, instead of making lactic acid. How does this help them survive?
column14: Making ethanol gives the fish about 36 ATP per glucose
column15: The ethanol releases oxygen into the fish's cells
column16: Making ethanol lets the fish do photosynthesis under the clear ice
column17: Ethanol leaves through the gills, so no acid builds up inside
column28: Either kind of fermentation gives only 2 ATP per glucose, so the advantage isn't more ATP. Lactic acid would build up inside the fish, but ethanol can be released through the gills, so the fish can keep running glycolysis and fermentation for days. A common mistake is thinking alcoholic fermentation makes more ATP than lactic acid fermentation.
column29: Both kinds of fermentation make the same ATP. What's different about where each waste product ends up?
